intro: Stokowski’s Philadelphia recording dates from 12 November 1934. The complete first disc side of the third movement is preserved here; only the common opening is aligned with Monteux’s complete 1942 movement.
question: How long can the opening melody breathe before the movement turns towards its dance?

sections.label: Renewed weight before the side ends

cues.title: Philadelphia before San Francisco
cues.text: The source dates Stokowski’s session to 12 November 1934 and first release to 1935. This file is part 1 of the third movement; the later sides remain separate.
cues.evidence: Commons description for HMV DB2525 / 2a84519 gives the session, release and side content.

cues.title: The early broad crest
cues.text: The opening’s largest measured crest extends across several windows. Follow the long phrase through its changing weight, rather than judging its pace by the number of new attacks.
cues.evidence: The strongest relative-level windows are 0:50–1:05, with the highest at 1:00. This is a contour within Stokowski’s transfer, not a cross-recording loudness claim.

cues.title: Less weight after the crest
cues.text: The continuation loses recorded weight after the crest without becoming silent. Compare how much time the melodic line receives here when you switch to Monteux.
cues.evidence: The 1:14 boundary accompanies a decline from −4.9 dB at 1:00 to about −11 dB at 1:15–1:30. Switching uses the provisional common-opening map.

cues.title: Beyond the shared opening
cues.text: The late part of this side gathers weight again before the side ends. The alignment deliberately stops before this stretch; no later entrance is assigned to the Monteux timeline.
cues.evidence: At the 3:12 boundary relative level rises from −13.9 dB at 3:00 to −6.9 at 3:20. The accepted comparison trim ends at 175 seconds.

facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
